prompt: Write 10 distinct lessons the mortgage-underwriting agent (residential mortgage applications and remortgages) at Larkmere Mutual learned across many cases about: flood and the mortgage valuation. Each is a working pattern or tip for the next case, not about any one member, one or two sentences, in the agent's voice ("When…, …"). Return {"items": [{"type": "fact" | "preference" | "observation", "content": "..."}]} with exactly 10 items. (batch 0)
response: {"items":[{"type":"observation","content":"When the postcode is flagged for flood, I treat the mortgage valuation as a starting point rather than the full picture, because the valuer may not have captured local drainage, river levels, or surface water routes."},{"type":"fact","content":"When a valuer notes flood risk but still recommends lending, I check whether the concern is about access, recurring damage, or insurability, because those points affect mortgage suitability differently."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the valuation is based on a drive-by or limited inspection, I ask for more recent flood information before I rely on it, as a brief visit can miss signs of previous water ingress."},{"type":"fact","content":"When there is any hint of flood history, I look for evidence that the property has remained saleable and mortgageable after the last event, because marketability matters as much as the physical repair work."},{"type":"preference","content":"When the applicant has a flood report or the valuer references a flood map, I prefer to see the date and source clearly, because outdated or generic mapping can overstate or understate current risk."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the valuation mentions standard construction but the area has known surface water issues, I do not assume the building form removes the risk, because even well-built homes can be affected by repeated water entry."},{"type":"fact","content":"When flood risk is seasonal or weather-related, I compare the valuation date with recent conditions, because a dry-period inspection can produce a more optimistic view than one taken after prolonged rain."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the valuer comments on insurance availability, I treat that as a material signal, because a property that is difficult to insure often becomes difficult to support with a mortgage as well."},{"type":"preference","content":"When the report is vague, I prefer to ask a simple follow-up on whether the concern is river, coastal, groundwater, or surface water, because the underwriting decision is usually clearer once the source is identified."},{"type":"fact","content":"When flood risk is raised at valuation, I always separate short-term inconvenience from long-term lending risk, because temporary disruption is not the same as a property that is likely to suffer repeated loss or reduced value."}]}
